definitions.meaning: Ernest Dowson's best-known poem is addressed to a woman of this name ('I have been faithful to thee, ... in my fashion')
the botanical genus of the globe artichoke and cardoon

explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions side by side: a literary one (the heroine of Ernest Dowson's poem) and a botanical one (the artichoke genus).
explanation.definitionFit: The same Latin word names the woman of Dowson's famous poem and the plant genus containing the globe artichoke.

clue.text: Right implement with which to demolish a faggot?

definitions.text: Right implement with which to demolish a faggot?

parts.words: Right implement with which to demolish a faggot?
parts.note: a faggot is both a bundle of firewood sticks, cut up with an axe, and a meatball eaten with Oriental eating sticks

explanation.walkthrough: A faggot is a bundle of sticks, which you might chop; it is also a British meatball, which could be eaten ('demolished') with Oriental eating sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: One of a pair of thin eating sticks used in East Asian cuisine to eat food such as a meatball.

parts.note: a roadside sign that is a white bar on a red disc looks like a minus sign; by the way means beside the road

explanation.walkthrough: 'by the way' means on the road, not 'incidentally': the road sign forbidding entry is a white horizontal bar, like a minus sign, on a red circle.
explanation.definitionFit: The traffic sign barring vehicles from a road shows a white bar, a minus sign, on red.

parts.note: a recurring decimal keeps repeating its digits, and the habit is that repeating

explanation.walkthrough: A recurring decimal such as 0.333... repeats its digits forever, so its 'habit' is repetition.
explanation.definitionFit: Repetition, happening again and again, is the habit of a decimal like one third written out.

clue.text: Sailor at a wild riot that becomes a shambles

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is the usual crossword sailor

indicators.note: a wild riot is one out of control, so these letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A sailor on shore leave joins a riot that turns into chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' before 'wild' is a link, and 'wild' turns RIOT into TOIR. 'Shambles' is meant in its old sense of a meat market or slaughterhouse, not a mess.
explanation.definitionFit: A shambles was originally a butchers' street or slaughterhouse, which is exactly what this French-derived word means.

clue.text: Have a yen for a singular property

definitions.meaning: read as two words, ..., to want

explanation.walkthrough: Split as BE LONGING, the word means 'have a yen for'; as one word, singular, it is one possession. A yen here is a craving, not the Japanese currency.
explanation.definitionFit: Split, the word means to be craving; whole and singular, it is one possession owned.

clue.text: Fare of course for the seafarer

definitions.meaning: hard ship's biscuit or food generally
a sailing ship's course relative to the wind

explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link. Sailors' food (hard tack, ship's biscuit) and a sailing ship's course against the wind share the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors called their ship's biscuit by this word, and a zigzag course into the wind is the same.

parts.note: to have the pip is to be grumpy, but a pip is also the star worn on a military shoulder to show rank

explanation.walkthrough: 'Got the pip' is British slang for being fed up, but a pip is also a star on an army uniform marking rank, such as a lieutenant's.
explanation.definitionFit: Army commissioned ranks are shown by pips, small stars on the shoulder, so the wearer is commissioned.

clue.text: What Russell made with the three Rs is even less done

parts.note: three copies of the letter R, spaced out
the Irish poet George William Russell signed his work with the pen name AE; the A comes first
the second R
the second letter of his signature AE
the third R

explanation.surface: Bertrand Russell's ideas on basic schooling were even more unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: George William Russell, the Irish poet, signed himself AE; interleave its two letters with the three Rs. 'Even' is a link; 'less done' is meat cooked for a shorter time.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat that is cooked for less time than another is more underdone, closer to raw.

clue.text: Common child who needs change of heart to attain a title

indicators.note: the middle of the word must be altered, so its central letters change places

parts.note: Bart is the abbreviation for baronet, a hereditary British title

explanation.surface: A lowly-born urchin must reform his ways to become a lord.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse runs backwards: swap the central letters of the answer to reach BART, the baronet's title, so the title read with its heart changed gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A brat is a badly behaved child, and common hints at a vulgar, ill-mannered one.

parts.note: a convertible motor is one whose roof folds down; once that has been done it has been turned into an uncovered vehicle

explanation.walkthrough: A convertible car, once 'converted' by folding the hood back, is a car without a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: A roofless motor vehicle is what a convertible becomes when its hood is lowered.

clue.text: A light character in a box

definitions.text: A light character in a box

parts.words: A light character in a box
parts.note: an old brand of friction match, kept in a matchbox, shares its name with the fallen angel, a character of light

explanation.walkthrough: An old word for a friction match, which lives in a box, is also the name of the Devil, the 'light-bringer'.
explanation.definitionFit: An early friction match was called by the Devil's name, which itself means bringer of light.

clue.text: What the rain might be doing to Peterborough district?

definitions.text: What the rain might be doing to Peterborough district?

parts.words: What the rain might be doing to Peterborough district?
parts.note: Peterborough sits on the edge of the flat, low-lying Fens of eastern England, where heavy rain soaks the ground through

explanation.walkthrough: Peterborough lies by the Fens, low marshy land in eastern England; rain falling on it would be soaking it completely.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain that wets land until it can absorb no more is soaking it through completely.

definitions.meaning: the maple genus; race here means a family or kind
a server who wins the point outright with an ace, as in tennis

explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' is a botanical family here, not a contest: the maples form this genus. The second reading takes an ace, the unreturnable serve, and makes a person who serves one.
explanation.definitionFit: The maple genus bears this Latin name, and one who serves aces would be a winner of points.

parts.note: these are ornamental ribbons or tassels tied right up at the hilt of a blade

explanation.walkthrough: 'Up to the hilt' means completely, but here it is literal: the ornamental tassels sit tied at the hilt of a blade.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornamental tassels or loops of ribbon tied to the hilt of a sabre are decorative features.

parts.note: the climber is a plant that clings to walls, and the bit is one piece of its foliage

explanation.walkthrough: The 'climber' suggests a social or mountain climber, but it is the evergreen plant that clings to walls, and its 'bit' is a single leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: A single leaf is one small part of the familiar clinging evergreen plant.

parts.note: an exquisite, as a noun, is an overdressed dandy, so this is how such a dandy behaves

explanation.walkthrough: 'Exquisite' looks like an adjective meaning beautiful, but as a noun it is an affected dandy, so this means like a dandy.
explanation.definitionFit: An exquisite was a vain, overdressed man, a dandy, so behaving like one is done vainly and affectedly.

indicators.note: the naturalist's name, once got at or tampered with, has its letters changed about

explanation.surface: The naturalist Charles Darwin showed real courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got' here means 'got at', interfered with, so the letters of DARWINS are rearranged; 'guts' is the intestines, not courage.
explanation.definitionFit: Inwards is an old plural noun for the entrails or innards of an animal.

definitions.meaning: read as lay men, men of the lay, a lay being a song

explanation.walkthrough: 'Laymen' are not the non-clergy here: a lay is a song, so lay-men are singers.
explanation.definitionFit: Singers, whether songbirds or people, make melody, and a lay is an old word for a song.

clue.text: "Here's a health unto his Majesty", naturally

definitions.text: "Here's a health unto his Majesty", naturally

parts.words: "Here's a health unto his Majesty", naturally
parts.note: the loyal toast to the monarch is drunk from a royal drinking vessel, and naturally points to a wild flower of the same name

explanation.walkthrough: The toast suggests a royal drinking vessel, but 'naturally' says the answer is the plant: the marsh marigold, a yellow wild flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The marsh marigold, a bright yellow wetland flower, is known by a name that also reads as a royal drinking vessel.

parts.note: 'the grey mare is the better horse' means the wife rules the house; a mare is a horse, a nag, and a domineering wife scolds

explanation.walkthrough: From the proverb 'the grey mare is the better horse', a dominant wife; a mare is a horse or nag, so being true to type means scolding.
explanation.definitionFit: Persistent scolding or complaining is what a domineering wife does, and a nag is also a horse.

clue.text: Granny no such relative to a king

definitions.text: Granny no such relative to a king

parts.words: Granny no such relative to a king
parts.note: a granny is a simple knot; the knot linked with King Gordius of Phrygia, which Alexander cut, was nothing like as easy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Granny' and 'relative' suggest family, but a granny is a knot, and the knot named after King Gordius was famously impossible to untie.
explanation.definitionFit: The intricate knot tied by King Gordius, cut by Alexander, gives its name to any problem of great complexity.

clue.text: A desert fighter is possibly authentic I conclude

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: possibly signals the word for authentic may be set down a little differently, with one letter shifted

parts.note: authentic means real
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier in the desert is perhaps the real thing, I decide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' shifts the E in REAL to give RAEL, set between IS and I; 'conclude' is a link. The desert is the Negev.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier from Israel, a country with much desert, is a desert fighter.

definitions.meaning: at English public schools, junior boys who did chores for seniors had this name
cigarettes, which are lit by the matches of 11 across

explanation.walkthrough: Two senses: junior pupils who served older boys at British boarding schools, and cigarettes, set alight by the old matches named at 11 across.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang names both cigarettes and the junior schoolboys who ran errands for seniors with this word.

parts.note: a guy is the effigy of Guy Fawkes burnt each year on the ... of November in Britain

explanation.walkthrough: A 'date with a guy' sounds romantic, but the guy is the Guy Fawkes effigy burnt on Bonfire Night, the fifth of November.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonfire Night, when Britons burn a guy, falls on this day of November.

clue.text: Alternatives to brief bags for the female members?

definitions.text: Alternatives to brief bags for the female members?

parts.words: Alternatives to brief bags for the female members?
parts.note: bags are trousers, so brief bags would be shorts; the female alternative is short garments worn by women, the members being legs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' is old slang for trousers, so 'brief bags' are shorts; 'members' are legs, and women might show them off in very short skirts instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Very short skirts are a woman's counterpart to shorts, exposing the legs much as brief trousers would.

parts.note: this abbreviates the word for this present month or moment, as in old business letters dated the 5th of this month

explanation.walkthrough: 'The time now' is 'instant', meaning this month in commercial letters; 'is short' says the answer is its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbreviation of instant, used in old business letters to mean the current month.

parts.note: a kid is a youngster
d was the abbreviation for an old British penny, a copper coin

explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is not a policeman but a penny, abbreviated d in old British money; 'as' is a link. Captain William Kidd was a notorious pirate.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain William Kidd was a seventeenth-century Scottish privateer hanged for piracy, a freebooter.

clue.text: A swimmer even with breath in him may be only middling good

indicators.note: the breath goes inside him, so one piece sits within the swimmer

parts.note: a fish is the archetypal swimmer
breath is air drawn in

explanation.surface: A swimmer with a lungful of air may still be only average.
explanation.walkthrough: 'even with' is a link, and 'in him' is the container signal: the swimmer holds the breath. 'Middling good' describes something passable, neither poor nor excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Something passable but not especially good is moderately fair, neither poor nor excellent.

clue.text: European, an untidy type, goes East

parts.note: a sloven is a habitually untidy person
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A messy foreigner heads off eastwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes' is a link joining the untidy type to E.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Slovenia, a central European country, is a European.

parts.note: peak means lofty, and holidays are festive days; together they make the phrase for great festive occasions

explanation.walkthrough: 'Peak holidays' sounds like busy holiday seasons, but read word by word it is lofty days, the phrase for festival occasions, as in 'high days and holidays'.
explanation.definitionFit: Festival days or special occasions are lofty days of celebration, as in the phrase about holidays.

parts.note: the dropped-aitch 'he's' is written as plain 'e's
in the nursery rhyme, Simple Simon met a pieman and wanted to taste his wares

explanation.surface: Someone says he sees that he has what Simon wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got' is a link. Simple Simon, in the nursery rhyme, met a pieman going to the fair and asked to taste his wares.
explanation.definitionFit: To espy is to catch sight of, so this verb form means notices or sees.
